suggestions.title: American History X
suggestions.description: With 113 titles now through this portal, this is the highest-rated film left anywhere in your database and the one real hole in your 1990s shelf, which currently holds Pulp Fiction, Fight Club, Goodfellas, Heat, The Silence of the Lambs, The Usual Suspects, Saving Private Ryan, The Big Lebowski, The Matrix, The Truman Show and Leon. Directed by Tony Kaye from an original screenplay by David McKenna, financed and released by New Line Cinema in October 1998, 119 minutes, shot by Kaye himself, cut by Jerry Greenberg, scored by Anne Dudley (of Art of Noise), and built on a formal device that never lets up: the present is in colour, every memory is in high-contrast black and white, so the film's argument is literally made in two stocks. Edward Norton is Derek Vinyard, a Venice Beach neo-Nazi leader who goes to prison for murder and comes out three years later wanting to pull his younger brother Danny (Edward Furlong) off the same road; Beverly D'Angelo is their mother, Avery Brooks the principal who assigns Danny a history paper on his brother, with Elliott Gould, Fairuza Balk and Stacy Keach around the edges. Norton was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actor, and the film carries a genuinely notorious production history: Kaye publicly disowned the released cut, tried to have his credit replaced with the DGA pseudonym Alan Smithee, and was himself shooting a documentary about the making of his own film - an argument the studio eventually won. It is brutal, and it is not subtle, but it is the most serious American film of the decade about how hate is inherited, and it ends on a bathroom wall. IMDb 8.5.

suggestions.title: Sunset Boulevard
suggestions.description: Your noir shelf so far is Double Indemnity and the Hitchcock set (Psycho, Rear Window); this is the noir that turns around and looks at Hollywood itself. Billy Wilder directed and co-wrote with his long-time partner Charles Brackett and D.M. Marshman Jr. - the last of the Wilder-Brackett collaborations, and the one that won the three of them the Academy Award for Best Story and Screenplay. Paramount, August 1950, 110 minutes, photographed by John F. Seitz, cut by Doane Harrison and Arthur Schmidt, scored by Franz Waxman. The structure is the thing: the picture opens with a body face-down in a swimming pool and the voice-over belongs to the corpse, a broke screenwriter named Joe Gillis (William Holden) narrating his own death backwards. Gloria Swanson - a real silent-era star, the actress Erich von Stroheim directed in the 1920s - plays Norma Desmond, a forgotten star of the silent screen living in a decaying mansion with her butler Max, who is (in the film's cruellest joke) von Stroheim himself, and who used to be her director and her husband. Cecil B. DeMille plays DeMille, Hedda Hopper plays Hedda Hopper, and Buster Keaton, H.B. Warner and Anna Q. Nilsson turn up for a card game as themselves. Eleven Academy Award nominations, three wins (screenplay, black-and-white art direction, score), and among the first 25 films placed on the National Film Registry in 1989. AFI ranked it the 12th greatest American film in 1998 and 16th in the 2007 revision. Norma's "I am big. It's the pictures that got small" and "All right, Mr. DeMille, I'm ready for my close-up" are in the language now. IMDb 8.4.

suggestions.title: The Thing
suggestions.description: Your horror shelf is The Shining, Alien, Get Out, Hereditary and The Conjuring, and this is the closest cousin Alien has: an isolated crew, one organism, no help coming and no way to tell who is already gone. John Carpenter directed; Bill Lancaster wrote the screenplay from John W. Campbell Jr.'s 1938 novella Who Goes There? (published under the pseudonym Don A. Stuart), which Howard Hawks had already filmed in 1951 as The Thing from Another World and which Carpenter deliberately went back past - his version restores the novella's shape-shifter, whose horror is that anybody can be it and the only test is a dish of blood. Universal released it on 25 June 1982, 109 minutes, shot in anamorphic widescreen by Dean Cundey, scored by Ennio Morricone - and stuffed with physical effects by Rob Bottin, who did the bulk of the creature work himself and was hospitalised with exhaustion on it, with Stan Winston's team quietly brought in for the dog-kennel sequence. Kurt Russell is MacReady, with Keith David, Wilford Brimley, Donald Moffat, Richard Dysart, Charles Hallahan, David Clennon, T.K. Carter, Richard Masur, Joel Polis, Peter Maloney and Thomas G. Waites filling out the station. It arrived two weeks after E.T. with a ~$15 million budget and took about $19.6 million; critics who had just been given a lovable alien called it the most repulsive film of the year, and it lost money. Four decades of home video and reconsideration later it is the benchmark for practical effects and one of the best American horror films of its decade - and it is a Carpenter you don't have. IMDb 8.2.
